summary: Provides definitions for Capacity and Available Capacity for IP traffic between a source and destination. A shared vocabulary helps build and test measurement tools. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines what network capacity and available capacity mean when counting IP traffic. It requires measurement results to identify the packet type and time interval so readers can interpret them.

questions: what is the narrow link and tight link
subtitle: Shared definitions for measuring IP-layer capacity and available capacity

tldr.problem: Capacity can refer to different things at different protocol layers, making measurement results difficult to compare. Available capacity also changes with traffic and time.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines IP-layer bits, link and path capacity, usage, utilization and available capacity for a specified packet type and measurement interval.
tldr.outcome: It provides a common vocabulary for capacity metrics; it does not define a measurement protocol or a particular tool.

facts.label: IP-layer bit count
facts.value: 8 times the octets in the IP header and payload

today: RFC 5136 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines capacity terms and does not specify a protocol.

sections.title: Why Capacity Needs a Shared Meaning
sections.content:
Capacity is not a single value that applies at every network layer. Encoding, framing, error correction and contention can all affect how much IP information a link carries. A signal frequency is not necessarily the same as the rate of information carried.

Capacity can also vary over time as traffic and link conditions change. The RFC therefore defines capacity in terms of a particular protocol layer and a stated measurement interval, giving researchers a common basis for comparing estimation methods.
sections.plainLanguage: A link's physical signal rate does not tell you how much IP data it carries. To compare capacity measurements, you need to say which layer and time interval you measured.

sections.title: Links, Paths and Physical Capacity
sections.content:
A node is a host, router, switch or other device where incoming and outgoing links may differ. A link connects two nodes, and a path is a series of links from a source to a destination. A single link is a path of length one.

Nominal Physical Link Capacity is the theoretical maximum supported by a link at the physical layer. The RFC gives an OC-3 link at 155.520 Mbit/s as an example. This value provides an upper bound; it does not determine the RFC's IP-layer capacity definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: A path is made of links between network devices. Its physical capacity is an upper limit, not a measurement of how much IP traffic arrives.

sections.title: What Counts as IP-Layer Bits
sections.content:
IP-layer bits are eight times the number of octets in correctly received IP packets, counted from the first octet of the IP header through the final payload octet. The count is made at the destination over an interval beginning at time T and lasting I; both T and I accompany any reported value.

Packets that cannot be passed to IP because of lower-layer errors, or that fail IP-header validation, do not count. Higher-layer headers need not be valid, IP options are included, and valid IP fragments count because they use link resources. The metric also identifies a Type P packet or flow class, since networks may treat packet types differently.
sections.plainLanguage: The count includes the IP header and payload of each packet received correctly. A result must say when and for how long it was measured, and what kind of packets it covers.

sections.title: Capacity, Usage and Available Capacity
sections.content:
IP-type-P link capacity, C(L,T,I), is the maximum IP-layer bits that can be sent from source to destination over a link during the interval, divided by the interval length. Path capacity is the capacity of the lowest-capacity link on the path. Link usage is the actual rate of correctly received IP-layer bits from any source, and utilization is usage divided by capacity.

Available link capacity is C multiplied by one minus utilization. Available path capacity is the smallest available link capacity along the path. The RFC calls the link with the lowest capacity the narrow link and the link with the lowest available capacity the tight link. Available capacity varies more, so a series of measurements may better characterize it.
sections.plainLanguage: A path's capacity is limited by its lowest-capacity link. Available capacity depends on how much of each link is already in use, so it can change over time.

sections.title: Sampling and Interpreting Results
sections.content:
Internet traffic varies across time scales, so the interval and sampling method matter. Sampling at a frequency that matches an underlying repeating condition can bias a result. Hardware-generated duplicate packets count in the general definition, although a Type P definition may restrict the metric to uniquely sent packets.

The RFC distinguishes its IP-layer definitions from Bulk Transfer Capacity, which measures unique application data at the transport layer using a congestion-aware connection. A BTC measurement is useful for a different purpose and does not correspond to the capacity values defined here. Measurement tools may themselves affect network security, privacy or performance.
sections.plainLanguage: A measurement can mislead if its timing misses normal traffic changes or counts duplicates differently than intended. Bulk Transfer Capacity answers a different question because it measures application data, not all IP-layer bits.

viz.caption: How the capacity terms are related

items.title: Link capacity
items.text: Maximum IP-layer bit rate over one link.

items.title: Usage
items.text: Actual IP-layer bit rate received on a link.

items.title: Available link capacity
items.text: Capacity multiplied by one minus utilization.

items.title: Available path capacity
items.text: The lowest available link capacity on the path.
